details.html: Add when combining alternatives that cannot happen to the same plant. For example, all tall offspring are either tall/green or tall/yellow, so their combined probability is 9/16 + 3/16 = 12/16 = ¾. Multiplication combines the independent requirements here; addition combines the non-overlapping categories. Neither operation is justified merely by seeing the word “and” or “or” without checking the events.

details.html: For specified independent events, multiply probabilities. Two recessive offspring in a row from Aa × Aa have probability 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Do not confuse this ordered event with “at least one recessive among two,” which asks for a different set of outcomes.

sourceReferences.relevance: The lesson contrasts two successive recessive offspring (solved1/16) with at least one recessive among two (named but not solved). With two independent1/4 events the latter has the same7/16 mathematics as candidateMC2; count unit differs (offspring versus loci).

sourceReferences.kind: fully solved component / source-defined video fallback, no playback
sourceReferences.content: For AaBb × AaBb, the A locus gives a 3/4 dominant-phenotype probability and 1/4 recessive probability. The B locus gives the same. If the loci assort independently, the probability of both dominant phenotypes is 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16. The other phenotype combinations are 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16, producing the familiar 9:3:3:1 expectation. This ratio is specific to the stated heterozygote cross and allele relationships. For a different cross, recompute. In AaBb × aaBb, probability of A_ is 1/2 and probability of B_ is 3/4, so both dominant phenotypes have probability 3/8. A memorized 9/16 would be wrong.
sourceReferences.relevance: Both-dominant9/16 explicitly solved; all three other phenotype class probabilities supplied. No7/16 union or homozygous-at-both aggregate.

record.prompt: Assume independent assortment and complete dominance at both loci. What phenotype ratio is predicted for TtYy × TtYy?

record.explanation: Each locus predicts a 3:1 phenotype ratio. Multiplying independent probabilities gives 9/16, 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16.

record.cue: Identify the relevant mechanism or quantity and apply the stated model.
record.explanation: P(A_) = 3/4 and P(bb) = 1/4; their product is 3/16.

record.prompt: Use a complete-dominance example to show why one phenotype can have two possible genotypes.
record.model: If B is completely dominant to b, both BB and Bb can produce the dominant phenotype. A dominant appearance therefore does not distinguish those genotypes. Only bb produces the recessive phenotype in the stated simple model.
